items.q: Which patient profile meets the page's listed reasons to start metformin in pre-diabetes?
opts: Age 40–60 years, HbA1c ≥6%, FBS ≥110 mg/dL and overweight
Age under 20 years with HbA1c below 5.7%
Normal weight with FBS below 100 mg/dL
Any age with isolated low triglycerides
items.exp: The page lists age 40–60 years, HbA1c ≥6%, FBS ≥110 mg/dL and overweight under starting metformin. (Book p920)

items.q: Match the pre-diabetes intervention to the page's note — 1) Metformin 2) Metformin in the pregnancy note 3) Pioglitazone 4) Pioglitazone mechanism … A) Start in the listed high-risk profile B) Treat gestational diabetes C) Added drug that acts through PPAR-γ D) Fights insulin resistance
items.exp: The treatment notes list metformin for the specified high-risk profile and for gestational diabetes, and add pioglitazone through PPAR-γ to fight insulin resistance. (Book p920)

items.q: What fasting blood-sugar value is listed as a reason to start metformin in pre-diabetes?
items.exp: The metformin list includes FBS ≥110 mg/dL. (Book p920)

items.q: Assess the pioglitazone notes: I The page says it slows cardiovascular risks. II The page says it decreases the risk of stroke.
items.exp: The pioglitazone column states that it slows cardiovascular risks and decreases the risk of stroke. (Book p920)

items.q: Which is the odd one out among the listed adverse effects of pioglitazone?
items.exp: The page lists bladder cancer, pathological fractures in osteoporosis and salt-water retention as adverse effects; hyperthyroidism is not listed. (Book p920)

items.q: A person belongs to the page's pre-diabetes screening group because of a prior pregnancy-related glucose disorder. How often is screening written for this group?
items.exp: The screening heading states that screening indicated in ADA guidelines is once in 6 months and includes gestational DM. (Book p920)

items.q: Match the screening indication to the exact group named — 1) Gestational DM 2) Pre-diabetic population 3) High-risk population 4) General population … A) 50% chance of developing diabetes B) Pre-diabetes C) Stroke, cardiovascular disease, HIV, PCOS or insulin-resistance signs D) Age ≥35 years
items.exp: The screening flowchart lists gestational DM with a 50% chance of diabetes, pre-diabetic population, high-risk conditions, and population ≥35 years. (Book p920)

items.q: The page lists three screening tests: HbA1c, FBS and ___.
items.exp: The screening-tests branch names HbA1c, FBS and PPBS. (Book p920)

items.q: Which screening test is described as having the best sensitivity and specificity for pre-diabetes?
items.exp: The HbA1c subsection calls HbA1c the best sensitivity and specificity test for pre-diabetes. (Book p920)

items.q: The HbA1c note is said to reflect approximately how many weeks of control?
items.exp: The page writes 6–8 week control below HbA1c. (Book p920)

items.q: Assess HbA1c limitations: I It provides only average values over a long period. II Ideal glycemic control at the target range for 70% of time requires 24-hour monitoring.
items.exp: Both statements are written in the HbA1c limitation note: average long-period values and 70% target-range time requiring 24-hour monitoring. (Book p920)

items.q: Match the HbA1c interference group to the printed examples — 1) Lower or increase 2) False lower value 3) False elevated value … A) Hemoglobinopathies, malnutrition B) Hemolytic anemia, blood loss, chronic liver disease C) Renal failure, iron-deficiency anemia, increased bilirubin and triglycerides
items.exp: The table lists haemoglobinopathies and malnutrition under lower or increase, haemolytic anaemia/blood loss/chronic liver disease under false lower, and renal failure/iron deficiency/increased bilirubin and triglycerides under false elevated. (Book p920)
